title: Mat Armstrong's one-off Oakley Veyron: a $1.2 million non-runner revived with pocket-change parts
dek: A carbon-bodied, 1,200 hp Veyron that sat dead in a Dubai showroom ran again after about $54 of fixes, but Bugatti's parts wall has slowed the finish.

car.trim: Oakley Design one-off (carbon body, 1,200 hp); model year not confirmed (2006 taken from service history dating to 2006)

source.where: A showroom in Dubai, shipped to England
source.boughtNote: The $1.2 million is how Autoblog and Supercar Blondie report the price from the first episode; Autoblog puts it at about $1.3 million with shipping and import duty. WhichCar gives $1.67 million with no currency, so the figure is not fully settled.
source.title: clean
source.damage: Non-running and not crashed. It started and then cut out, selected gears only some of the time, had perished in-tank fuel hoses, a faulty ignition switch and key, a bad repair with high resistance in the pyrofuse wiring, and an airbag light on. Later it needed brake pads that Bugatti would not sell.

episodes.t: I BOUGHT A NON RUNNING BUGATTI VEYRON
episodes.what: Armstrong buys the one-off Oakley Design Veyron in Dubai and gets it running with fuel hoses, an ignition switch, a resistor and small parts, then has it valued by Tom Hartley Jnr.

episodes.t: BUGATTI REFUSED TO SELL US THE FINAL PART SO WE MADE IT
episodes.what: The title says the team made the last part themselves after Bugatti would not sell it; we found no reporting on which part it was.

parts.part: Submersible in-tank fuel hose and correct clamps
parts.why: The original hoses had perished, and the hoses fitted in Dubai used the wrong clamps, so the car cut out
Part of the electrical repairs (Autoblog, AutoNext)

parts.part: Key battery and pyrofuse wiring repair
parts.why: Faulty original key; a bad earlier repair left high resistance in the battery-disconnect circuit

parts.part: Front and rear brake pads (bought online, shipped from the U.S.)
parts.why: Bugatti would not sell pads without its own bedding-in procedure, quoted at about £50,000
Bugatti would not sell it, according to the October 18 video title

time: Bought and first fixed by the September 6, 2026 episode. Brake pads in mid-September, a new fault in mid-October, and the made-in-house final part on October 18. About seven weeks over two main-channel episodes plus one on Mat Armstrong MK2.

costs.note: Bought is the reported $1.2 million. Other is an estimate of about $100,000 for shipping and UK import duty, from Autoblog's ~$1.3 million all-in figure. Parts are the reported ~$54 first-round fix plus the £1,500 brake pads, converted at ~1.33 USD/GBP to about $2,000. The made-in-house part is not included because its cost is unknown. Labour is Armstrong's own and is not counted.

value.basis: Tom Hartley Jnr valued it at £1.5 million (about $2 million at ~1.33 USD/GBP). Standard Veyron 16.4 sales in 2025-26 ran from $1.35 million (a higher-mileage BaT car) to about $2.23 million at RM Sotheby's, against CLASSIC.COM's ~$1.96 million benchmark. The range is trimmed at the low end for the one-off body and non-factory parts. It has a clean title, so no salvage discount applies.

verdict: On paper it already pays. About $1.3 million all-in buys a one-off Veyron that a leading UK dealer values at £1.5 million (about $2 million). The repairs have so far cost pocket change. The lesson is not that Veyrons are cheap to fix. It is that a car written off as "non-running" can be stranded by a $14 switch and a perished hose, and a buyer who can diagnose that can buy below the market. The open risks are ownership costs, a one-off body that narrows the buyer pool, and non-factory parts in a world where Bugatti controls the service history.
body:
## The buy

Mat Armstrong already owned one Bugatti Veyron when he was offered a second, non-running one sitting at the back of a showroom in Dubai. He flew out from England, inspected it for about twenty minutes and bought it [3]. This is no ordinary Veyron. It is a one-off Oakley Design car. Every body panel except the doors was redone in exposed carbon fibre, the car is about 100 lb lighter than standard, and a retune lifted the quad-turbo W16 from roughly 1,000 hp to 1,200 hp [4][5].

Autoblog and Supercar Blondie both report the price from the first episode as $1.2 million [3][4]. Autoblog puts the total at about $1.3 million once shipping and UK import duty are added [3]. WhichCar, an Australian site, gives $1.67 million without naming the currency [8]. AutoNext says only that it was a seven-figure sum [5]. No outlet gives a model year. Dealer Tom Hartley Jnr said he knew the car's history back to 2006 [3], so we list it as a 2006 car. That year is our inference, not something stated in the reporting.

## The damage

The car was not crashed. Hartley found no accident record [3], so it is not a salvage-title car. It had stopped working, and the reported faults were these:

- It would turn over, start briefly and then cut out [4][8].
- It would only select a gear some of the time [4][5].
- Its in-tank fuel hoses had degraded, which AutoNext blames on ethanol in the fuel [5]. Armstrong had diagnosed the same fault on his first Veyron [3].
- Wiring in the battery-disconnect (pyrofuse) circuit had been badly repaired and had too much resistance [4][5].
- The ignition switch and original key were faulty [8].
- An airbag warning light was on [8].

Before shipping, a Dubai prep company that had watched Armstrong's earlier video replaced the fuel hoses. The car ran when it arrived in the UK. Then it died again, because the wrong clamps had been fitted [3][4].

## The work and the parts

Armstrong redid the hose job himself with submersible-rated fuel hose and proper clamps. AutoNext puts the hose at about €12 [5]. He traced the no-start to the ignition switch, which turned out to be a Volkswagen Transporter part costing about $14 [3]. He also fitted a resistor costing about $4 and a pair of bonnet gas struts from a VW Tiguan [3][5]. He fixed the pyrofuse wiring and fitted a new battery in the original key [5][8]. The reported total for the first round of fixes ranges from about $54 to $74, or £40 (€46), depending on the outlet [3][4][5][8].

The brakes were next. Armstrong said Bugatti would not sell him front and rear pads for the car. His parts contact told him the pads need a bedding-in procedure that must be done at Bugatti. The dealer route was quoted at around £50,000 (about $67,000) [6][7]. MotorBiscuit says that claim was not independently verified [7]. Armstrong bought a new set online and had it shipped from America for £1,500 (about $2,000) [6][7]. That episode ran on his second channel, Mat Armstrong MK2 [6].

In mid-October Bugatti invited Armstrong to Molsheim with both his Veyrons. Shortly before the trip the Oakley car developed a new fault, and he had to leave it in the UK [9]. On October 18 the main channel posted an episode titled "Bugatti refused to sell us the final part so we made it" [2]. We found no reporting that says which part he made or how. We are not guessing.

## The money

Counting the reported $1.2 million price, about $100,000 for shipping and import duty, roughly $54 of first-round parts and about $2,000 of brake pads, the car stands at about $1.3 million [3][6].

On the other side of the ledger, Hartley valued the car at £1.5 million, which Autoblog converts to about $2 million [3]. Public sales of standard Veyron 16.4 coupes back that up. RM Sotheby's sold an 8,000-mile 2008 car at Monterey in August 2026 for $2,232,500. RM sold a 3,000-mile 2006 car in Miami in February 2026 for $2,122,500. A 20,000-mile 2006 car brought $1,350,000 on Bring a Trailer at the end of 2025. CLASSIC.COM's market benchmark for the EB 16.4 sits near $1.96 million [10]. A Mansory-modified 2008 car made $2,365,000 at Mecum in January 2026 [10], which suggests heavily altered Veyrons are not automatically marked down.

A salvage or rebuilt title usually takes 20 to 40 per cent off a car's value. This Veyron has no record of crash damage [3], so that discount should not apply. The risks are different ones. A one-off carbon body narrows the pool of buyers. Pads that did not come through Bugatti could matter to a buyer who wants factory service history.

Running costs matter too. In 2019 The Drive reported an annual fluid service of about $25,000, tyres at about $38,000 a set every two to three years, and a fuel tank job at $42,000 [11].

## What's next

Armstrong told Hartley he is keeping the car [4]. In mid-October it had a new, unexplained fault [9], and the October 18 episode says the team made the last part Bugatti would not supply [2]. The car is still in progress until we see it driven and sorted. The next things to watch are whether it gets to Molsheim and what Bugatti's own technicians say about it.
